Brown Street Drugs

By: Graham Coetzer | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
we investigate the notorious Brown str in the Pretoria cbd, just a few blocks from the Union Buildings, where drug dealers run amok and the police seem unable to stem the tide

Summary:
Brown str in the Pretoria cbd has a rich history as the starting point for many anti apartheid marches pre 1994. Currently it's become infamous as a drug mecca, with a large number of drug dealers selling the addictive Nyaope - a mixture of Heroin and a host of other chemicals. What is surprising is how openly the the dealers operate, the huge amounts of deals done on a daily basis, and the failure of the city's authorities to stop the whole process.

Further information:
We have been filming the deals happening in Brown str since June this year. We have a lot of footage showing the constant deals happening - literally hundreds a day. Although there seems to be a lot of police activity, our footage shows that police are not following procedures, are not making arrests and raises serious questions around possible police corruption. We have met two Nyaope users, car guards who work outside the North Gauteng High Court, who are willing to expose the dealers. The users buy "hits" of Nyaope netween 3 - 5 times a day. The Nyaope is mixed with tobacco and dagga and smoked. The users admit their addictions have driven them to a life of crime or begging on the streets, and point fingers at both Tshwane Metro and Pretoria Central SAPS members, who they say do not arrest the dealers, but rather take bribes from to look the other way. Several business owners in the area are also suspicious of the police's involvement, and say that since the arrival of the dealers in the area, their businesses have suffered under an ever growing crime wave fueled by addicts desperate for cash.

Press Release:


Nyaope Street
Drug addicts wanting a quick fix know that Brown Street in Pretoria’s CBD is the place to go to. Among the filth and litter, drug dealers and users roll joints laced with heroin and a cocktail of lethal ingredients, commonly known as Nyaope. Carte Blanche takes you into the heart of this notorious street, home to dealers openly plying their trade, while police seem to turn a blind eye.


Script:


Brown Street
22 Oct 2014
First Draft Script

Voice
Meet John and Michael, not their real names, two severely addicted heroin users from Pretoria.

Sound Up “Michael”
Devi: So this is “zol” right?
Michael: “Zol”, and this is the packet.
Devi: And what is this?
Michael: This is nyaope, heroin.

Voice
There is a misconception that Nyaope is a specific type of drug – it’s not. It’s simply a mixture of heroin, marijuana and tobacco.

Sound Up “Michael”
Devi: So wait, how much was this?
Micheal: This was 35.
John: Each.

Voice
R35 will buy you enough heroin for one joint – it’s cheap, dirty and highly addictive.

Sound Up “Michael”
Devi: How many like that do you smoke a day?
Michael: Maybe four or five per day,
John: It depends with the money.

Voice
Nyaope has become the drug of choice for many addicts in Pretoria, mainly because it’s relatively cheap and easy to get hold of. The drug is so popular it’s literally flooding the city’s streets.

Link Devi
This is Brown street, a few blocks down the road from the Union Buildings. It’s an open secret in Pretoria – if you want drugs, you make a stop here.




Voice
We sent our cameramen, disguised as builders, into an abandoned building along Brown street. From a concealed position a few floors up we could stake out the dealers, users and passersby outside the various businesses along the alley. Our cameras caught literally hundreds of deals going down in broad daylight.

Sound Up Dewald Te Brugge
I was in the police in the narcotics bureau, and this is a problem area since 1997, since I was in the police, Brown Street was a problem area.

Voice
Dewald te Brugge is a private investigator who spent 15 years as a member of the now disbanded SANAB – the South African Narcotics Bureau. After seeing our footage, Dewald said the situation in Brown street had deteriorated.

Sound Up Dewald Te Brugge
When I was in the police I worked with stuff like this but never on a big scale like this, it’s actually scary to see how these people are dealing in open day light.

Voice
This man, who we’ve dubbed Mr. Blue, is one of the dealers and particularly active along Brown street. Mr Blue starts his day from as early as six in the morning, when the first addicts looking for a fix arrive. By midday, Mr Blue and his friends are doing a roaring trade.

Sound Up Michael
Nyaope is like it’s a bad devil. You can’t see it but it tells you to do things. When you are alone you feel it, I have to find Nyaope.

Voice
Michael and John wanted to show us just how easy it is to buy Nyaope at Brown str, and offered to wear a hidden camera on one of their daily shopping trips. The footage shows them buying heroin from several dealers. Their final stop is at a dealer who sells rolling papers, marijuana and loose cigarettes to add into the mix.

Sound Up Michael and John
Devi: Guys we’ve just come back from Brown str, so what did you get?
Michael: Small packet of heroin, and weedy, cigarette and Rizla.
Michael: You put the saliva so it can’t go fast, fast, fast. It must go slow, slow, slow.

Voice
Various media reports have claimed that Nyaope contains anything from rat poison to Anti Retroviral Drugs or ARVs. We arranged for a sample from Brown street to be tested at the University of Pretoria’s Department of Chemistry.

Sound Up Dr Tim Laurens
Brown street was 37% of heroin, and also 31% of caffeine.

Voice
Dr Tim Lourens heads up the university’s Forensic Toxicology Laboratory. Tim believes reports of Nyaope containing ARV’s have been exaggerated.

Sound Up Tim
They claim that it’s mixed with ARVs or perhaps sometimes even metal oxides from fluorescent lights. Well I think in that case the person will only pick up heavy metal poisoning. But I think that is more a myth then that it is actually the truth.

Voice
But the mixture of drugs in Nyaope remains a highly addictive cocktail. Michael and John say their addictions have led them to a life of crime.

Sound Up Michael & John
Michael: You’ll do anything, you’ll grab anything, you’ll even grab cell phone and run away.
Devi: So you’ve been arrested before?
Michael: Ja, many times.
Devi: For what?
Michael: Possession of drugs, possession of what what, stealy-stealy, maybe steal someone’s phone, but after I find this job for car guarding, no more stealy.

Voice
The never ending drug supply from hotspots like Brown street are fueling crime waves across the city. The 2014 crime statistics show a 230% increase in drug related crimes in the Pretoria CBD over the past 5 years. One example of how drugs fuel crime in the city can be found at Schubart Park.

Sound Up Wimpie Basson
They’ll literally come to you and they tell you, listen you can build your fence, you can do what you want, but we will come in here and we will steal the steel because we want to sell it to smoke that nyaope.

Voice
Wimpie Basson is a building contractor working on the refurbishment of Schubart Park in the city center. In September 2011 the city of Tshwane evicted residents from the blocks of flats as they had become unsuitable for habitation. But when Wimpie and his crew arrived on site a few weeks ago, they were confronted by groups of men stripping the buildings of any steel.


Sound Up Wimpie Basson
Devi: How many were here?
Wimpie: Some days there were 15, some days there were about 25. One day there were about 50 guys in here.

Voice
John admits that stolen metal, sold to scrap yards, is an easy way to feed his habit.

Sound Up John
Devi: Schubart Park, what’s happening there?
John: Me, I was there Saturday. I went to take some steel. You see if you don’t have anything you can hustle with you can go Schubart, you take some steel, you know you gonna find thirty bucks to buy some drugs you see.

Voice
The Brown street dealers don’t seem too bothered about where their clients get their money – as long as they’re buying product. This dealer, who we’ve dubbed the Sweeper, often pretends to be cleaning the city’s streets. But that’s obviously not how he’s making his living. Based on deals captured on our footage we estimate the Brown street dealers could be making as much as R30 000 to R50 000 a day.

Sound Up Spook
The problem is if you arrest one dealer today, tomorrow there is two in his place.

Voice
This is warrant officer Spook van den Berg. Spook heads up the Pretoria Central police station’s war on drugs, and he holds the record for the most arrests in one month by a single police officer. But he admits it’s an uphill battle.

Sound Up Spook
Spook: if I arrest a guy for possession of dagga, or possession of heroin, it goes to court the next day, then that evidence has to be sent to a lab to concur, yes, that is heroin, or yes that is cocaine or yes that is dagga. Tomorrow morning the case will get withdrawn temporarily against that suspect and he gets released out back onto the street.

Voice
The police have no choice but to release suspects until the results of the drug tests are made available

Sound Up Spook
Devi: How long does it take before you get the results back?
Spook: It’s supposed to take 6 weeks but our labs have a backlog of a year and a half at this stage.


Sound Up M & J
Devi: Are there certain policemen who are involved with this?
Michael: some policemen they don’t want to go, they say we’re still waiting for bribe, if you don’t give bribe you can’t sell, up until they give money to go.

Voice
On this morning we saw a Pretoria Central vehicle, with the call sign PC80, stop in front of Mr Blue and others, including this man in the striped shirt. Two policemen order the dealers into the back of the vehicle and they drive off. We have confirmed that PC80 did not return to the police station. Within the hour the vehicle returns, seemingly to drop the dealers off, and once they’ve left its business as usual for Mr Blue and his team.

Sound Up Dewald
The South African Police Service is not a taxi service. So what are they loading them for? If you load someone into a vehicle it’s procedure to have them searched for weapons because that’s how policemen get killed on duty.

Voice
Michael and John say they’ve seen this before, and believe there’s nothing legit about this police activity.

Sound Up John
John: The dealers they can climb into the van and then the cop can go at the back, “no I want 1000 for all of you here.” They bring the 1000 so they can unlock and go.

Voice
This footage shows a vehicle from the K9 unit drive slowly up Brown str and stop beside the dealers. The police are approached by this man who we filmed selling drugs ,who leans into the vehicle for a few seconds. As soon as he’s done the vehicle drives off.

Sound Up Dewald
Devi: If you were the police would you arrive at Brown Street in a marked vehicle wanting to collect intelligence?
Dewald: No, that’s not normal, intelligence you wouldn’t even meet with your informer nearby there, you’ll get your informer somewhere else, and definitely not in a marked vehicle or in uniform.
Devi: Suspect behaviour?
Dewald: Suspect behavior – that’s 100 percent.

Voice
The police have denied our request for an interview, but in a written response they said they had identified Brown Street as an area that needed special attention from law enforcement. On the 15th of October SAPS, Metro Police and officials from various government departments descended on Brown Street. One of the dealers was caught with 40 sachets of heroin and heroin rocks to the value of R11 000 were found on the street. The police said corruption by members of the police wouldn’t be tolerated and the South African Police Service would do all in its power to investigate. They also said operations in the area were ongoing.

Sound Up Spook
You have to have equipment and manpower to go after the guy who brought it in.

Voice
Meanwhile the Brown street dealers continue unabated and they have started bringing new products onto the market.

Sound Up Spook
There’s a new pill I found in Brown street, it’s R350, R400 depends on how much you buy. It consists of heroin, ecstasy and kat. You can smoke it or you can inject it but it’s extremely lethal.

Voice
Dewald believes specialized units like SANAB should be reinstated to wage the war on drugs and take on the people who make their living from the trade.

Sound Up Dewald
The problem is only getting bigger and bigger and bigger, it’s getting out of hand. It’s like a market, a flea market, you can just openly go and buy, it’s an open for all.

Sound Up Spook The problem is if you arrest one dealer today, tomorrow there is two in his place. Voice This is warrant officer Spook van den Berg. Spook heads up the Pretoria Central police station’s war on drugs, and he holds the record for the most arrests in one month by a single police officer. But he admits it’s an uphill battle. Sound Up Spook Spook: if I arrest a guy for possession of dagga, or possession of heroin, it goes to court the next day, then that evidence has to be sent to a lab to concur, yes, that is heroin, or yes that is cocaine or yes that is dagga. Tomorrow morning the case will get withdrawn temporarily against that suspect and he gets released out back onto the street. Voice The police have no choice but to release suspects until the results of the drug tests are made available Sound Up Spook Devi: How long does it take before you get the results back? Spook: It’s supposed to take 6 weeks but our labs have a backlog of a year and a half at this stage. Sound Up M & J Devi: Are there certain policemen who are involved with this? Michael: some policemen they don’t want to go, they say we’re still waiting for bribe, if you don’t give bribe you can’t sell, up until they give money to go. Voice On this morning we saw a Pretoria Central vehicle, with the call sign PC80, stop in front of Mr Blue and others, including this man in the striped shirt. Two policemen order the dealers into the back of the vehicle and they drive off. We have confirmed that PC80 did not return to the police station. Within the hour the vehicle returns, seemingly to drop the dealers off, and once they’ve left its business as usual for Mr Blue and his team. Sound Up Dewald The South African Police Service is not a taxi service. So what are they loading them for? If you load someone into a vehicle it’s procedure to have them searched for weapons because that’s how policemen get killed on duty. Voice Michael and John say they’ve seen this before, and believe there’s nothing legit about this police activity. Sound Up John John: The dealers they can climb into the van and then the cop can go at the back, “no I want 1000 for all of you here.” They bring the 1000 so they can unlock and go. Voice This footage shows a vehicle from the K9 unit drive slowly up Brown str and stop beside the dealers. The police are approached by this man who we filmed selling drugs ,who leans into the vehicle for a few seconds. As soon as he’s done the vehicle drives off. Sound Up Dewald Devi: If you were the police would you arrive at Brown Street in a marked vehicle wanting to collect intelligence? Dewald: No, that’s not normal, intelligence you wouldn’t even meet with your informer nearby there, you’ll get your informer somewhere else, and definitely not in a marked vehicle or in uniform. Devi: Suspect behaviour? Dewald: Suspect behavior – that’s 100 percent. Voice The police have denied our request for an interview, but in a written response they said they had identified Brown Street as an area that needed special attention from law enforcement. On the 15th of October SAPS, Metro Police and officials from various government departments descended on Brown Street. One of the dealers was caught with 40 sachets of heroin and heroin rocks to the value of R11 000 were found on the street. The police said corruption by members of the police wouldn’t be tolerated and the South African Police Service would do all in its power to investigate. They also said operations in the area were ongoing. Sound Up Spook You have to have equipment and manpower to go after the guy who brought it in. Voice Meanwhile the Brown street dealers continue unabated and they have started bringing new products onto the market. Sound Up Spook There’s a new pill I found in Brown street, it’s R350, R400 depends on how much you buy. It consists of heroin, ecstasy and kat. You can smoke it or you can inject it but it’s extremely lethal. Voice Dewald believes specialized units like SANAB should be reinstated to wage the war on drugs and take on the people who make their living from the trade. Sound Up Dewald The problem is only getting bigger and bigger and bigger, it’s getting out of hand. It’s like a market, a flea market, you can just openly go and buy, it’s an open for all. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): we investigate the notorious Brown str in the Pretoria cbd, just a few blocks from the Union Buildings, where drug dealers run amok and the police seem unable to stem the tide
metadata.Summary: Brown str in the Pretoria cbd has a rich history as the starting point for many anti apartheid marches pre 1994. Currently it's become infamous as a drug mecca, with a large number of drug dealers selling the addictive Nyaope - a mixture of Heroin and a host of other chemicals. What is surprising is how openly the the dealers operate, the huge amounts of deals done on a daily basis, and the failure of the city's authorities to stop the whole process.
metadata.Further information: We have been filming the deals happening in Brown str since June this year. We have a lot of footage showing the constant deals happening - literally hundreds a day. Although there seems to be a lot of police activity, our footage shows that police are not following procedures, are not making arrests and raises serious questions around possible police corruption. We have met two Nyaope users, car guards who work outside the North Gauteng High Court, who are willing to expose the dealers. The users buy "hits" of Nyaope netween 3 - 5 times a day. The Nyaope is mixed with tobacco and dagga and smoked. The users admit their addictions have driven them to a life of crime or begging on the streets, and point fingers at both Tshwane Metro and Pretoria Central SAPS members, who they say do not arrest the dealers, but rather take bribes from to look the other way. Several business owners in the area are also suspicious of the police's involvement, and say that since the arrival of the dealers in the area, their businesses have suffered under an ever growing crime wave fueled by addicts desperate for cash.
